data.title: Nvidia ($NVDA) Loses $500 Billion in Market Value as CEO Scandal Rattles Investors
data.description:
Chipmaker Nvidia (NVDA) has lost $493 billion in market value over the past week amid a scandal that resulted in CEO Jensen Huang resigning on Nov. 12. Nvidia's market capitalization declined $182 billion in the previous trading session after Huang announced his resignation shortly before the stock market opened.

Shares of Nvidia have fallen nearly 30% in the past month as the company has been rocked by reports Huang engaged in extramarital affairs, including with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. As recently as September, Nvidia had a market capitalization of more than $5 trillion and was the world's most valuable publicly traded company.

Nvidia's key performance indicators. Source: TipRanks

Nvidia Slips Down the Rankings

The maker of powerful artificial intelligence (AI) microchips and processors was the first company in history to achieve a $5 trillion market cap. But now, Nvidia's market capitalization sits at $4.01 trillion and it has been surpassed by Apple (AAPL) and Microsoft (MSFT).

Analysts warn that Nvidia's stock may have further to fall as the repercussions from the Chinese spying scandal continue. The chipmaker might be sued by shareholders over the wealth destruction caused by Huang' actions while leading the company.

Nvidia's Upcoming Earnings

More immediately, Nvidia's stock is likely to be tested on Nov. 17 when the company reports its third-quarter financial results. Executives on the earnings call are likely to be peppered with questions about the scandal and what comes next for Nvidia.

Some analysts say it will also be important for Nvidia to get the appointment of its next CEO right and reassure Wall Street that the company and its growth remain on track. A disappointing CEO pick will further erode confidence in Nvidia and send its share price lower, warn some market observers.

Is NVDA Stock a Buy?

Nvidia's stock has a consensus Strong Buy rating among 36 Wall Street analysts. That rating is based on 28 Buy and eight Hold recommendations issued in the past three months. The average NVDA price target of $262.62 implies 59% upside from current levels.
data.author: Joel Baglole

data.title: NIO's Margin Recovery Is No Longer Enough to Justify a Buy
data.description:
NIO (NIO) stock's margin recovery is no longer enough to justify a Buy rating, in my view, as the company continues to face pressure on deliveries and demand. Trading near $3, the Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker's American Depositary Receipt (ADR) has lost more than half its value since its April high and is now hovering near its 52-week low.

What's interesting is that this is happening even as vehicle margins have improved significantly, reaching 18.5% in Q2, up 8.2 percentage points year-over-year. However, domestic EV demand in China remains under pressure, while fierce competition is becoming a structural headwind.

In my view, betting that these improved margins will hold up has become riskier. Without a consistent recovery in deliveries, I see little reason to remain bullish, even with the ADR looking cheap. For now, I prefer a neutral stance.

NIO's Demand Problem Goes Beyond China's EV Slowdown

Let's start with one of the biggest concerns weighing on NIO shares: weakening demand.

China's EV demand is under significant pressure, but NIO's slowdown cannot be blamed entirely on the broader market. Third-party data shows that domestic retail sales of new-energy vehicles fell 13.7% year-over-year in October, marking a tenth consecutive monthly decline.

Still, battery-electric vehicle sales fell by a milder 5.3%, while new energy vehicles (NEVs) reached a record 67.5% share of China's passenger-car market. So it's clear that electrification continues to gain market share, even as overall demand weakens.

Competition is another sensitive issue, separating winners from losers. Peers such as XPeng (XPEV) delivered 50,237 vehicles in October, up 19.6% year-over-year, while Leapmotor (HK:9863) exceeded 106,000 deliveries. NIO, meanwhile, delivered 34,246, down 15.2%, ending 31 consecutive months of annual growth. The decline was far from uniform. Breaking it down by brand, ONVO deliveries plunged 51.7%, while the premium NIO brand still grew 5.7% and Firefly rose 30.9%.

Overall, the most positive aspect is that NIO's total deliveries are still up 38.5% through October. So the slowdown is not yet evidence of a company-wide collapse. However, since the market tends to look ahead, ONVO's struggles suggest the company is having a harder time scaling its more affordable lineup. This raises questions about whether NIO can sustain its margin recovery without stronger delivery growth.

Margin Recovery Has Been Years in the Making

Speaking of margins, the big question now is whether NIO can sustain its recovery if deliveries remain under pressure.

To put this in context, vehicle margins — which are essentially the gross margins on new vehicles — have historically been one of NIO's biggest challenges. After reaching more than 20% in early 2021, driven mostly by higher average prices and economies of scale, they collapsed to just 5.1% in Q1 2023. This was driven by a less favorable product mix, discounts on older models, and, above all, intense competition in China's EV market.

The recovery was gradual. Lower material costs helped vehicle margins improve to 12.3% in 2024 and 14.6% in 2025. Yet the real turning point came in late 2025, when stronger demand for higher-margin models, combined with further cost cuts, pushed margins to 18.1% in Q4.

How Much Longer Can NIO's Margins Offset Weakening Demand?

This margin recovery continued into 2026. In Q2, vehicle margins reached 18.5%, up from 10.3% a year earlier. This was largely driven by premium SUVs such as the ES8 and ES9, both of which carried margins above 20%, according to management.

That being said, what matters now is how much longer these margins can offset weakening demand. In my view, not indefinitely. Even with a still-strong vehicle margin in Q2, NIO generated just RMB 207 million in adjusted operating profit, while remaining unprofitable on a GAAP basis.

This leaves NIO vulnerable to a prolonged decline in deliveries, especially since premium models like the ES8 and ES9 have also started losing momentum. Unless NIO can stabilize volumes or further reduce operating costs, even margins near 20% may not be enough to sustain its profitability recovery. That seems to be what the market is pricing in.

NIO's Valuation Leaves Little Room for Weakening Demand

With NIO trading around $3, I think traditional valuation multiples only tell part of the story. What matters more is how close the business is to generating sustainable operating profits.

Consider that in Q2, NIO generated roughly RMB 5.38 billion in vehicle gross profit across 107,658 deliveries, or about RMB 50,000 per vehicle. Including gross profit from other operations and assuming the same cost structure, my calculations suggest NIO would need approximately 38,200 monthly deliveries to break even on a GAAP operating basis.

That's not particularly far from October's 34,246 deliveries. Yet even a small change in volumes could make a big difference. At 40,000 monthly deliveries, quarterly operating profit could reach around RMB 270 million, while 45,000 deliveries could push that figure above RMB 1 billion. Of course, these are simplified scenarios assuming Q2 margins, product mix, and expenses remain unchanged. With China's domestic EV market still under pressure, I see few reasons to expect a sharp rebound in NIO's deliveries anytime soon.

There is also value beyond vehicle sales. The recent Geely (GELYF) deal valued NIO's battery-swapping subsidiary at approximately RMB 16 billion, providing an external reference for an asset often overlooked in traditional valuations.

To me, the current $8.46 billion market capitalization doesn't necessarily look excessive. However, it still requires investors to believe NIO can recover volumes without sacrificing its improved margins. That's precisely where my conviction has become more cautious.

Is NIO a Buy, According to Wall Street Analysts?

Wall Street's NIO forecast remains fairly optimistic, with the ADR carrying an overall Moderate Buy consensus rating. Of the 11 analyst ratings issued over the past three months, six are Buy, four are Hold, and just one is Sell. The average NIO price target currently stands at $5.76, implying a massive upside potential of roughly 89% from current levels.

NIO's Margin Recovery Isn't Enough to Stay Bullish Anymore

NIO has made real progress, especially on margins, but the bigger picture is becoming harder to ignore. Demand is weakening, and competition remains fierce. That leaves NIO's profitability dependent on too many things going right from now on. At around $3, the ADR certainly looks tempting. Yet cheap stocks can always get cheaper, especially when structural headwinds are at play — and there's little reason to believe they will disappear overnight.

For now, I'd rather take a more cautious stance than bet on a turnaround that still has plenty to prove. So I'm downgrading NIO's ADR to Hold.
data.author: Bernard Zambonin

data.title: Oracle (ORCL) Faces a Cash Crunch, but Its AI Bet Still Looks Promising
data.description:
Oracle (ORCL) faces a cash crunch, but its artificial intelligence (AI) bet still looks promising. Best known for its database software, the company has become one of the biggest builders of AI data centers. Its capex is at a record high. Now the obvious question is whether Oracle can earn a decent return on it all.

I'm bullish on Oracle. Demand for its AI cloud keeps growing, and management has finally put a date on its cash problem. At today's price, much of the bad news already looks priced in. However, it is not entirely a safe bet.

Oracle stock is down about 34% this year, even though revenue grew 30% last quarter and adjusted earnings beat estimates. The worry is that Oracle is spending far more cash than it brings in, and borrowing heavily to do it. However, I believe its latest moves show a realistic way out.

Oracle's AI Demand Is Real

Oracle's AI demand is real, and the latest quarter shows it. Its cloud infrastructure business, which rents out computing power, grew revenue 121% to $7.4 billion. Oracle also delivered 850 megawatts of new AI capacity to customers, almost triple the previous quarter's. Its graphics processing units (GPUs), the chips that run AI models, were in use 97.9% of the time.

The detail I like most comes from renewals. GPUs whose contracts ended were renewed or resold at a 20% premium, even though most of them were at least four years old. That eases a common fear that AI hardware loses its value quickly.

More growth is already under contract. Oracle's remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached $664 billion. RPO is the value of signed contracts that haven't turned into revenue yet, and Oracle expects about half of it to become sales within 36 months.

Oracle Is Building on Borrowed Money

Oracle is building much of its AI business on borrowed money, and that is its biggest problem. Last quarter, capex hit $28.5 billion, more than Oracle's entire revenue of $19.3 billion. That pushed free cash flow to -$5.4 billion. For the full fiscal year, management expects capex of $90 billion to $95 billion.

Oracle had about $125 billion of borrowings at the end of August, and its newest bonds pay 7% to 8.65% a year. On the plus side, Oracle's debt-to-equity ratio, or what it owes for each dollar that belongs to shareholders, fell to 2.34 from 4.36 a year earlier. That decline came from share sales and profits, not from debt repayment, which remains high. In July, S&P (SPGI) cut Oracle's credit rating to BBB-, one notch above junk.

This is where return on invested capital (ROIC) matters. It measures how much profit a company earns on all the money tied up in its business. Adding up TipRanks' figures for the last four quarters, I get about 9%, down from about 11% a year earlier. Earning about 9% while paying more than 7% on new debt leaves a thin cushion. That worries me most.

Customers are the other risk. OpenAI, Oracle's biggest customer, is still losing money. Microsoft (MSFT), meanwhile, is winding down a 2023 deal to rent AI capacity from Oracle, reportedly because the servers use older Nvidia (NVDA) chips that no longer meet its needs.

Oracle's Cash Problem Looks Fixable

Oracle's cash problem looks fixable to me, mainly because management finally has a plan. After its last quarterly report, management still wouldn't say when free cash flow would turn positive. That changed at its Investor Day in October. Oracle now expects positive free cash flow in the second half of Fiscal 2028 and more than $30 billion in Fiscal 2029.

To me, that is a good signal. Investors' biggest fear was that the spending had no end. Now there is a date and a number that management can be held to.

Oracle also capped new stock and bond sales through Fiscal 2030 at $20 billion and raised the full amount in early November, splitting it evenly between $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds. If it sticks to that cap, it shouldn't need more new money from investors.

New deals help, too. Last quarter, Oracle signed more than $30 billion of AI contracts that needed no extra cash from the company, mostly because customers paid upfront or brought their own hardware. I find that more reassuring than any long-term revenue target.

Is Oracle Stock a Bargain?

Oracle stock looks like a bargain to me, at least next to its own history. Its trailing-12-month (TTM) price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is about 20x, meaning investors pay about $20 for each dollar of reported profit Oracle made over the past year. At the end of each of the last five fiscal years, its P/E was between about 29x and 42x. Microsoft, another heavy AI spender, trades at about 27x.

The forward P/E, based on analysts' adjusted earnings estimates for the next 12 months, is about 15x. That is down from about 29x in late November 2025 and near its lowest since 2022. Analysts expect adjusted earnings per share (EPS) to grow almost 36% in Fiscal 2028. If so, about 15x looks cheap to me.

The main risk is execution. Oracle wants to more than triple its capacity by the end of Fiscal 2028, to about 10 gigawatts. If big data centers come online late, revenue and cash flow will arrive late, too.

How Does Wall Street See Oracle?

Wall Street is bullish on Oracle, with a Strong Buy consensus rating based on 28 Buys, four Holds, and one Sell assigned in the last three months. At $241.83, the average Oracle price target implies 90.26% upside potential.

Bernstein's Mark Moerdler, a five-star analyst on TipRanks, reiterated his Buy rating and $325 price target on November 10, implying about 156% upside. He sees two catalysts: more clarity on OpenAI's ability to pay for its computing commitments, and Oracle's return to positive free cash flow. His target looks too high to me, but I agree that free cash flow will decide where the stock goes next.

The Bottom Line

I'm bullish on Oracle. It is a good business in a tough spot. I usually avoid companies with this much debt and such thin returns on capital. Oracle stands out because it has a huge backlog of signed contracts and, now, a target date for positive free cash flow. If management delivers, today's price may look cheap in a few years.
data.author: Karol Kowalczyk

data.title: 3 Expensive Stocks Wall Street Still Loves
data.description:
Using the TipRanks Stock Screener tool, we identified three high P/E stocks with Strong Buy consensus ratings and average analyst price targets implying at least 22% upside. Despite their premium valuations, analysts see further growth potential driven by AI demand and company-specific catalysts.

Why Do Some Stocks Have High P/E Ratios?

A high price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio does not necessarily mean a stock is overvalued. Some investors are willing to pay a premium for companies expected to deliver solid earnings growth. Strong industry trends and competitive advantages can also justify higher valuations. However, investors must assess whether future growth can support the current valuation.

Monolithic Power Systems (MPWR)

  • P/E Ratio: 78.79x 
  • Average Monolithic Power Price Target: $1,778.57 (22.9% upside)

Monolithic Power Systems develops power-management chips that help electronic devices use electricity efficiently. Growing demand from AI servers, data centers, and other high-performance applications is supporting the company's growth outlook.

MPWR delivered strong third-quarter fiscal 2026 performance. Adjusted EPS came in at $8.19, versus analyst expectations of $7.79. Revenue rose 63.1% year-over-year to $1.20 billion, surpassing estimates of $1.16 billion. Growth was driven by strong demand from enterprise data and AI infrastructure, with enterprise data revenue surging 164.6% year-over-year. The company also raised its enterprise data growth outlook, highlighting continued momentum in AI-related demand.

Marvell Technology (MRVL)

  • P/E Ratio: 53.81x
  • Average Marvell Price Target: $323.63 (96.8% upside)

Marvell develops custom chips and networking products used in AI data centers. Major cloud companies are investing heavily in custom AI chips to reduce their dependence on standard GPUs. Marvell helps these companies design such chips and provides the networking technology needed to connect them across large data centers.

Marvell is scheduled to report its Q3 FY27 results on November 26. Wall Street expects Marvell to report adjusted earnings of $1.10 per share, up from $0.76 per share in the year-ago period. Revenue is projected to surge 52.2% year-over-year to $3.15 billion.

Block (XYZ)

  • P/E Ratio: 109.59x 
  • Average Block Price Target: $104.37 (26.9% upside)

Block is a fintech company that provides payment services for businesses through Square and financial services to consumers through Cash App. It also owns the buy-now-pay-later platform Afterpay.

Block surpassed both earnings and revenue estimates for Q3 FY26. Adjusted EPS came in at $1.13, versus analyst expectations of $1.03. Revenue increased 9.9% year-over-year to $6.72 billion, surpassing estimates of $6.59 billion. Growth was supported by strong performance across Cash App and Square, with Cash App gross profit rising 27% to $2.07 billion, driven partly by higher lending activity, while Square gross profit increased 14% to $1.16 billion.

data.title: Microsoft vs. Salesforce: One Software Stock Remains a Top Pick, the Other Has Something to Prove, Says RBC
data.description:
Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) sell to many of the same corporate customers, and both are betting that AI agents, software that can carry out tasks on its own, will become a major source of revenue.  

Today, Microsoft got an uncomfortable reminder of how much those customers rely on it. A global outage that started Thursday afternoon knocked Outlook and parts of Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services offline for millions of users, and it dragged into Friday after the first fixes didn't hold. Microsoft says it has found no sign of malicious activity.  

Microsoft shares are down around 1.5% in premarket trading on Friday. Salesforce has had a tough year of its own, with the stock down about 18% year to date.

RBC analyst Rishi Jaluria covers both tech giants and published notes on each this week, ahead of Microsoft's Ignite conference (November 17-20) and Salesforce's fiscal third-quarter report on December 2.

Microsoft

Starting with Microsoft, the analyst expects Ignite to show how far the company has pushed AI into every layer of its business, from data centers and in-house chips to apps and security. However, he doesn't see the event moving the stock much in the short term.

The backdrop is strong. Azure grew 48% in constant currency last quarter, up from 43% the quarter before, and management has guided for 49% to 50% this quarter. Jaluria believes demand still outruns the capacity Microsoft can bring online, which makes that guidance look cautious, though the year-ago comparison is a tough one. He wants updates on capacity and on Maia 300, the custom chip unveiled in October, which Microsoft is designing to be 40% more efficient than leading GPU setups and expects to roll out at multi-gigawatt scale in 2027.

Then there's Copilot. Daily users jumped about 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold year over year, while customers with over 50,000 Microsoft 365 seats grew more than 8x. Jaluria thinks investors are overlooking Microsoft's shift toward usage-based pricing, which Cowork and GitHub Copilot already use. Charging for consumption rather than per user could lift the ceiling on what Microsoft earns as agents take on more work, and he expects Ignite to add new agent-building and management tools.

"Stepping back," Jaluria summed up, "MSFT continues to be our top pick, and we believe they are a differentiated AI beneficiary across the full stack. We see Ignite as an opportunity for management to further demonstrate the depth and breadth of AI monetization across the stack."

To this end, Jaluria rates MSFT as Outperform (i.e., Buy) with a $640 price target, a figure pointing to 12-month returns of 22%. (To watch Jaluria's track record, click here)

Microsoft gets a Strong Buy consensus rating on the Street, based on 35 Buys and 4 Holds. At $632.48, the average price target implies shares will gain 21% over the coming months. (See MSFT stock forecast)

Salesforce

Salesforce gets a cooler reception. Jaluria thinks software sentiment has yet to recover, and he lists Salesforce among the application companies without clear sight of a near-term growth pickup. That's not because the numbers are weak. Fiscal second-quarter (July quarter) revenue rose 11% YoY, cRPO grew 14% in constant currency, and net new annual order value (AOV) posted its best growth in four years. Agentforce ARR climbed to $1.5 billion, up more than 240%.

What he can't yet see is whether that momentum turns into lasting organic acceleration. Dreamforce left him slightly more upbeat. Its centerpiece, AI Force, opens Salesforce data, workflows and governance to outside AI tools through MCPs, APIs and plugins, on the argument that Salesforce's real value lies in the business context underneath, not the screens people click on. Jaluria isn't sure that holds up if AI model providers move into that territory, and easier outside access could eventually make Salesforce's own apps less essential. Partner checks also suggest pricing is still being worked out.

M&A is the other sticking point. Braze (about $5.66 billion), Cresta, Listen Labs and Rune Technologies push Salesforce's M&A spending over the past 12 months to roughly $27 billion by RBC's estimate. Each deal makes strategic sense, Jaluria says, but together they pile on integration risk just as investors want homegrown growth. He has worried about a return to "empire-building" since the Informatica deal.

The stock trades at about 12x RBC's calendar 2027 free cash flow estimate. "Valuation remains undemanding," says Jaluria, "but the sustained M&A cadence, early-stage AI monetization, and the need to cleanly integrate multiple concurrent acquisitions make it difficult to underwrite material upside in the near-term. In our view, Salesforce needs to demonstrate that this acquisition wave translates into durable organic reacceleration before the stock can re-rate."

To this end, he rates Salesforce as Sector Perform (i.e., Neutral) with a $250 price target. Still, should the figure be met, investors will be pocketing returns of 15% a year from now.

Eight other analysts join Jaluria on the sidelines, but with an additional 30 Buys, the stock claims a Strong Buy consensus view. Over the next year, shares are expected to appreciate by 29%, given the average price target stands at $280.41. (See CRM stock forecast)

data.title: SpaceX-Tesla Merger Talks Advance: Combined Value Nears $3.4 Trillion
data.description:
SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA) are moving closer to a potential merger that could become the largest corporate merger in history. According to a Bloomberg report, the two Elon Musk-led companies could announce the deal as early as December 2026, although talks could also extend into early 2027.

SpaceX has a market value of about $1.9 trillion, while Tesla is valued at around $1.5 trillion. Together, the companies have a combined market value of roughly $3.4 trillion. Tesla's annual shareholder meeting is scheduled for December 3, making it an important date for investors watching the talks.

Boards Work on Merger Terms and Structure

The boards and advisers of both companies are working on the terms of the proposed merger, including ownership and governance. One of the main points under discussion is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive in the deal.

Both companies have formed special committees of independent directors to review the proposed combination. Musk also described the merger as a "good idea" during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call in October.

Combined Business Would Span EVs, Space, and AI

A merger would bring Tesla's electric vehicles (EVs), energy storage systems, and robotics business together with SpaceX's rockets and satellite services.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a key part of the proposed combination. The companies could use their combined technology across self-driving cars, humanoid robots, and space-based services.

The two companies already have business ties through Terafab, a joint effort to build a semiconductor plant in Texas. The venture aims to produce its first test chip around May or June 2027, with full-scale production targeted for the third quarter of 2028, Musk said.

China and U.S. Security Rules Pose Challenges

Despite progress in talks, the merger faces regulatory hurdles. One concern is how Tesla's large manufacturing operations in China would fit into the combined business. SpaceX, meanwhile, holds U.S. government and defense contracts that involve national security concerns.

These differences could make regulatory and shareholder approvals more complex. Several analysts have suggested that the merger could also face greater political scrutiny after Democrats took control of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections.

TSLA or SPCX: Which Stock Do Analysts Prefer?

According to TipRanks' Stock Comparison Tool, SpaceX carries a Strong Buy consensus rating while Tesla has a Moderate Buy. Moreover, SPCX's average analyst price target implies a higher upside potential of 76.2%, compared with 5.4% for TSLA.
data.author: Sheryl Sheth

data.title: Buy Nvidia Stock 'With Both Hands,' Says Analyst as Valuation Drops to 'Stupid' Levels
data.description:
Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 4.3% on Thursday, closing at $166.19, following CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. However, Freedom Capital's analyst Paul Meeks urged investors to buy Nvidia stock "with both hands," saying its valuation has reached "stupid" levels.

Huang's resignation followed reports of a second affair, this time involving Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell. He had earlier admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national and Megaspeed executive. Nvidia has named current CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Nvidia's Valuation Falls

Since the Huang controversy gained traction, Nvidia shares have fallen 10.96% since last Friday, wiping out $492.8 billion in market value. The stock is now down 20% in November and about 30% from its all-time high. NVDA stock is up 2% in premarket trading on Friday.

Meeks noted that Nvidia stock is now trading at just 10 times its estimated fiscal 2028 earnings following Thursday's decline. Meanwhile, Nvidia trades at a forward GAAP P/E of 16.64, well below the sector average of 27.83. This ratio compares Nvidia's current share price with its expected earnings over the next 12 months, based on GAAP accounting rules.

Meeks has made bullish calls on Nvidia several times when its stock price fell. This is the first time he has backed the stock during a leadership crisis rather than a broader market sell-off.

Mizuho Securities technology analyst Jordan Klein also shared a bullish view earlier this week. He called Nvidia stock "ridiculously cheap" and said the decline could offer investors an attractive buying opportunity.

Meeks Remains Bullish on AI Growth

Meeks believes Nvidia's current share price does not reflect its long-term growth potential from AI and related technologies. He sees strong demand for its data center chips as a key driver. In Q2, Nvidia reported data center revenue of $89 billion, up 117% year-over-year.

Huang led Nvidia for more than 30 years, helping it become a leader in the AI industry. Meeks believes Nvidia's strength lies in its products, not its founder, and that the company can continue to grow without Huang at the helm. He said, "I think that the actual announcement of his resignation is a market-clearing event."

Matt Witheiler, head of late-stage growth private investments at Wellington Management, shared a similar view. He said: "The company's market cap reaching $4 trillion isn't because Jensen Huang is the CEO; it's because its revenue hit $100 billion last quarter, a year-over-year increase of 100%."

Nvidia Earnings Ahead

Nvidia is set to report its Q3 FY2027 results on November 17, after the market closes.

Wall Street expects Nvidia's revenue to jump nearly 91% to $108.72 billion from $57.01 billion a year earlier. Earnings are forecast to rise about 90% to $2.47 per share, up from $1.30.

Is NVDA Stock a Buy?

Nvidia's stock has a consensus Strong Buy rating based on 27 Buys and 10 Holds issued in the past three months. The average NVDA price target of $254.84 implies 53% upside from current levels.
data.author: Kirti Tak

data.title: Bloom Energy Stock (BE) Is Down 15% in 3 Months — Why HSBC Says It's a Buy
data.description:
Shares of Bloom Energy (BE), the U.S.-based solid-oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems developer, have fallen by roughly 15% over the past three months. However, HSBC analyst Samantha Hoh has added the stock to a list of 11 names to buy amid the recent sell-off in tech and industrial shares. Hoh set a price target of $350, implying about 73% upside from BE stock's Thursday closing price of $201.93. The analyst praised Bloom as "a leader" in SOFC with more than 90% market share and a profitable service model.

Why Bloom Energy Stock Has Sold Off Recently

Bloom Energy shares have recently been under pressure. The company recently reported a negative free cash flow of more than $180 million. This is despite its third-quarter earnings beat on both revenue and earnings per share.

Delays in a project involving Oracle (ORCL) have also contributed to the sell-off. In addition, BE stock plunged 16.41% on November 5 as AI stocks sold off on Democrats' midterm-election gains.

The election outcome sparked fears of stricter data center construction policies. This could impact demand for Bloom's fuel cell systems.

HSBC Is Bullish on Bloom Energy But Sees Risks

According to Hoh, Bloom dominates the market for baseload, behind-the-meter power solutions. In other words, the market provides stable electricity through power systems installed on customers' sites. The market covers systems that use natural gas, hydrogen, and biogas to generate electricity.

"With a profitable service model on an installed base of nearly 3GW across 1,100+ locations in 9 countries, Bloom is increasing its manufacturing capacity to serve data center demand," Hoh said in part.

Still, the analyst flagged key risks in Bloom's business:

  • The business is heavily concentrated in the U.S.
  • Chairman and CEO K.R. Sridha holds ownership and voting power.
  • There are concerns about delays in manufacturing capacity expansion or cost overruns. In other words, projects end up costing more than originally planned.

Is Bloom Energy a Good Stock to Buy Now?

On Wall Street, analysts remain cautious on Bloom Energy's shares, with a Moderate Buy consensus rating. This reflects 12 Buys and nine Holds issued over the past three months.

However, the average BE price target of $295 implies about 46% upside (see BE stock forecast here).

data.title: Stock Market Today, Nov. 13: U.S. Stocks Wobble Ahead of PPI Data
data.description:
U.S. stock futures traded mixed ahead of Friday's market open as investors awaited the release of October's Producer Price Index (PPI), a key measure of wholesale inflation. Economists expect prices to rise 0.4% in October, easing from September's 1.3% increase.

Futures on the Nasdaq-100 (NDX) were down 0.13%, while futures on the S&P 500 Index (SPX) and the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) were up 0.12% and 0.21%, respectively, as of 5:42 a.m. EST on November 13.

Meanwhile, Microsoft (MSFT) shares fell in premarket trading as engineers worked to fix server issues behind a global Outlook outage. The disruption affected businesses, governments, and individual users, with Outlook inaccessible through its app and website across parts of Asia and Europe. The outage began around 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and affected hundreds of thousands of users in the U.S.

Oil prices also fell on Friday, putting crude benchmarks on track for a second consecutive weekly decline. President Donald Trump said the U.S. did not need a deal with Iran to end the war, signaling that the blockade and economic sanctions would continue. While the risk of a wider conflict has eased, attacks on shipping remain a concern for Middle East oil supplies.

At the time of writing, Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 0.21% to $95.64 per barrel, while WTI crude futures were down 0.59% at $88.18 per barrel.

During Thursday's regular trading, all three major indexes closed lower amid concerns surrounding Nvidia (NVDA) CEO's exit. Huang co-founded the chipmaker and led the company for 33 years. His departure has drawn attention following allegations involving relationships with employees and claims about a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

The Nasdaq fell 0.39%, the S&P 500 declined 0.35%, and the DJIA lost 0.36%.

Investors are now looking to the PPI report for further clues about inflation and the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook. A reading above expectations could increase concerns about persistent inflation and influence the Fed's rate decisions. Earlier this week, October's Consumer Price Index (CPI) showed U.S. inflation rising 0.4% month over month, above economists' expectations of 0.3%.

Global Markets

European stocks retreated on Friday, while Asia-Pacific markets ended mostly lower as concerns surrounding Nvidia's leadership and broader weakness in technology stocks weighed on investor sentiment.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index declined 1.55%. In China, the Shanghai Composite fell 0.59%, and the Shenzhen Component was down 1.48%. Japanese markets bucked the broader regional trend, with the Nikkei 225 rising 0.53% and the Topix gaining 0.11%, even as the yen strengthened to 159.9 against the U.S. dollar.
data.author: Sheryl Sheth
